newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda starts stock exchange, no trading floor yet.
newsitem.headline: Uganda starts stock exchange, no trading floor yet.

text.p: The Kampala Stock Exchange will be officially launched in the Ugandan capital on Thursday but trading will be delayed because there is no trading floor, officials said.
Merchant bankers, prospective floor dealers, investors and government officials will meet at the Kampala Sheraton Hotel to start the market.
Prospective bourse players will go through the rules before the five companies allowed to open brokerage subsidiaries formally sign up, senior markets officials told Reuters.
Uganda privatisations team leader Otweyo-Orono told Reuters that Uganda Grain Milling Co would be the first to be listed on the bourse when trading finally opened.

But it was still uncertain when trading would begin. The East African Development Bank building in Kampala, which was due to house the bourse, is still under renovation. Authorities have no idea when the construction work will be completed.
"Since we have a core investor with Uganda Grain Milling Co, it will be the first to be traded when the exchange opens," Orono said. "But we don't have the logistics in place."
Orono said the next company would be Uganda Consolidated Properties Ltd -- but privatisation authorities were still seeking a strategic co-investor in the company.

Orono has previously listed 15 state companies as targeted for sale through a public flotation. These include Uganda Commercial Bank, Uganda Airlines, Uganda Posts and Telecommunications, Uganda Consolidated Properties, Uganda Grain Milling Co, Uganda Railways Corp and Dairy Corp.

The recent sale of part of the government's stake in Uganda Grain Milling Co sparked protests because the government ignored the highest bid -- from Kenya's Unga Ltd -- and offered the milling concern to Caleb International, a Ugandan company owned by a brother to Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni.

Simon Rutega, coordinator of capital markets at the (central) Bank of Uganda, said five merchant banks would open brokerage subsidiaries for the new market. A sixth had applied to offer brokerage services but had not yet met basic requirements.
"We are still on target. We finalised analysis of the business proposals and have now shortlisted members," he said.

The companies cleared to open brokerage subsidiaries are Stanbic Bank, Barclays Bank, The Merchant Bank of East Africa, NDC Capital Alliance and Trans Africa Bank, Rutega said. He said the choices were based on these companies' experience.
"The companies have international experience, credibility, capital requirements and confidence of the public; and we are confident that they will have a quality market," Rutega said.
He said Uganda Commercial Bank (UCB), which the government has listed for sale, had also wanted to offer brokerage services but had so far failed to meet some key requirements.
Market analysts saw the UCB application as strange because the government has said it will sell some of its shareholding in the bank through a public flotation on the Kampala bourse.

Minister of State (deputy minister) for privatisation Matthew Rukikaire told reporters last week that the government would inject $70-80 million in bonds into Uganda Commercial Bank in order to make it attractive to any serious buyers.

When trading begins, it will be by an open outcry system on the lines of the Nairobi Stock Exchange. An electronic settlement system is not in place and officials have left it to market players to decide on settlement when the bourse opens.
